Reclustering using the LR scores combined with gene expression separated FDCs from marginal 188 
reticular cells (MRCs), revealing two distinct signalling patterns of cell populations within the 189 
originally annotated FDCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e). The identities of FDCs and MRCs were 190 
validated using canonical marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 4f)21, and spatial mapping confirmed 191 
their respective localization, with FDCs restricted to germinal centres and MRCs positioned in the 192 
surrounding regions (Fig. 3d). 193 
 194 
To further characterise regional niches, we computed neighbourhood enrichment scores for each 195 
cell type (Fig. 3e). Unsupervised clustering on cell neighbourhood enrichment has clearly 196 
separated the germinal centres, B, and T cell rich zones. FDCs primarily communicate with 197 
germinal-centre cells, including Tfh and GC B, and plasma cells, whereas MRCs interact more 198 
broadly with naïve and memory B cells as well as pDC, mDC, and multiple T -cell subsets. 199 
Interestingly, macrophages showed no strong enrichment in any of those regions, contributing to 200 
regulation in all regions of the tonsil22.  201 
 202 
While FDCs and MRCs occupy distinct niches and differ in their interacting partners, they 203 
converge in specific signalling programs. Both express C3, a key complement component 204 
involved in antigen presentation23,24 (Fig. 3f), and MRCs additionally produce soluble regulators 205 
of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways25–28 (Extended Data Fig. 4j). 206 
 207 
We also discovered distinct LR interactions associated with FDCs and MRCs: Inside the germinal 208 
centres, FDCs and macrophages express the checkpoint ligands PD -L1 (CD274) and PD -L2 209 
(PDCD1LG2), positioning them to modulate Tfh cells through PD -1 (PDCD1) 29. FDCs also 210 
uniquely express WNT5A, which supports germinal-centre B-cell survival via non-canonical WNT 211 
signalling30; in our data, we identified FZD3 as the likely interacting partner. Interestingly, we found 212 
that GC B cells express high levels of PDGFD, which could influence the clonal expansion and 213 
differentiation of the PDGFRβ positive MRCs into FDCs31–34 (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). 214 
 215 
Outside the germinal centres, MRCs express TNFSF13B (BAFF), often considered a defining 216 
FDC product35,36. We found that FDCs within the germinal centres express very low levels (Fig. 217 
3e), consistent with flow cytometry and scRNA -seq data21. TNFSF13B is an essential survival 218 
factor for naïve B cells 35, although it is dispensable for germinal -centre B-cell survival37. In our 219 
dataset, macrophages and mDCs were also substantial sources of TNFSF13B, supporting their 220 
contribution to B -cell survival and differentiation. Lack of TNFSF13B leads to failure of FDC 221 
maturation; consequently, stimulation of B cells via immune complexes can not occur 38. Beyond 222 
their effects on B cells, MRCs help organise T cell -rich zones in the paracortex by secreting 223 
CCL19 and CCL21, chemokines that recruit CCR7-positive cells39, including T cells, NK cells, and 224 
mDCs in the tonsil. MRCs supply CSF1 and IL34 which are important growth factors required for 225 
the control of monocyte and macrophage differentiation, survival, proliferation, and renewal 40, 226 
suggesting their importance in macrophage development and differentiation outside of germinal 227 
centres. These findings highlight the importance of MRCs as tissue organisers in tonsil that signal 228 
to B cells, T cells, and macrophages shaping their  development, survival, and migration 229 
(Extended Data Fig.  4i). 230 
 231 
.CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 International licenseavailable under a 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made 
The copyright holder for this preprintthis version posted November 28, 2025. ; https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.11.26.690796doi: bioRxiv preprint 

To compare pathway-level communication between MRCs and FDCs, we performed a differential 232 
analysis of LR interactions between the two populations. The Gene Ontology (GO) analysis 233 
revealed both shared and distinct biological processes (Fig. 3h)41: For example, GO terms related 234 
to dendritic cell antigen processing and presentation were significantly enriched in MRCs, 235 
whereas the ERBB2 signalling pathway was enriched in FDCs. 236 
 237 
By applying LARIS to a human tonsil Slide -tags sample, we demonstrated that it can resolve 238 
distinct cell states within a cell type and identify the LR interactions enriched for those states. Its 239 
single-cell level scoring further guided the analysis by revealing spatially distinct communication 240 
patterns of FDCs and MRCs. LARIS recovered known LR pairs and connected them to sender 241 
and receiver cell types in the tonsil and suggested previously uncharacterised communications 242 
that influence cell survival, migration, and maturation. 243 
 244 
LARIS identifies region and time specific interactions in the developing mouse brain 245 
 246 
We next applied LARIS to map the spatiotemporal dynamics of LR interactions during mouse 247 
brain development, a process governed by spatially organized signalling cascades42. We focused 248 
on the cerebral cortex, a structure defined by its distinct layered architecture and corresponding 249 
functional and transcriptional heterogeneity43. 250 
 251 
To assess this we applied LARIS to Stereo -seq datasets collected at different developmental 252 
stages of the mouse brain, i.e., embryonic day (E)14.5, E16.5, postnatal day (P)7, P14, and P773–253 
5 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). We annotated the cortex as upper and deep layers for the 254 
postnatal samples, and for the prenatal samples we included additional developmental cell types 255 
(Fig. 4a). 256 
 257 
LARIS identified differentially enriched spatial LR interactions across mouse cortex development. 258 
For example, the Slit1::Robo1 interaction, known to modulates proliferation and neurogenesis44,45, 259 
axon guidance and neuronal migration 46,47, was restricted to upper layer neurons prenatally but 260 
present in both upper and deep layer postnatally (Fig. 4b). Another intriguing example, the 261 
Sema3c::Plxna4 interaction, which was most prominent in the migrating and deep layer neurons 262 
prenatally, yet only sporadically present in the postnatal cortex (Fig. 4b). Sema3a, a closely 263 
related ligand with similar structure and expression to Sema3c, regulates interneuron positioning 264 
via Plxna448. By contrast, the role of Sema3c in the developing mouse cortex remains unknown, 265 
raising the possibility of a Sema3c::Plxna4 signalling axis. 266 
 267 
To systematically analyse the LR interactions identified by LARIS, we grouped them by function 268 
(e.g., neurotransmitters, axon guidance, growth modulators, Wnt signalling) and plotted their 269 
strengths across developmental stages and cortical layers (Fig. 4c). This revealed clear stage -270 
specific activities patterns of different ligand -receptor pairs. For example, among the growth 271 
modulators, Igf2::Igfr2 49, Fgf15::Fgfr2 50, Mdk::Sdc1 51, Dlk1::Notch2 52, Jag1::Notch 53 were 272 
primarily enriched prenatally In contrast, Fgf1::Fgfr1, Fgf9::Fgfr1, Fgf20::Fgfr2, were predominant 273 
in the adult brain, likely contributing to neuronal maintenance54,55. 274

To connect these LR interactions to underlying biological processes, we performed Gene Set 276 
Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)41 on the differentially expressed LR pairs at different stages (Fig. 277 
4d). The results confirmed expected developmental trajectories: prenatal stages were enriched 278 
for gene function terms such as 'axon guidance', while the adult stage was dominated by 279 
pathways related to synaptic integration (e.g., 'neuroactive ligand -receptor interaction', 280 
'glutamatergic synapse', 'GABAergic synapse', and 'synaptic vesicle cycle').  281 
 282 
We also examined LR interactions along specific spatial axes. Along the dorsal -ventral axis, 283 
Slit1:Robo1, Efnb1::Epha4, and Lrfn5::Ptprs showed clear spatiotemporal dynamics (Fig. 4d). 284 
Along the rostral -caudal axis, we further identified multiple spatially restricted interactions 285 
(Extended Data Fig. 5b, c). For example, Aldh1a3, which encodes an enzyme that converts 286 
retinaldehyde into retinoic acid, was expressed at P7 specially in the caudal upper layer 287 
corresponding to the forming visual area. This pattern was confirmed by Allen Institute’s in situ 288 
hybridization (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Other examples include Cdh12:Itgb1 enrichment in the 289 
rostral cortex and Penk, an opioid polypeptide hormone, enrichment in the rostral deep layers 290 
postnatally (Extended Data Fig. 5b, c). 291 
 292 
Together, these spatiotemporal analyses on mouse cortex development demonstrated that 293 
LARIS can identify and characterise key signalling molecules and pathways underlying the 294 
complex intracellular and intercellular dynamics through development. 295 
 296 
Discussion 297 
 298 
Here we presented LARIS, a computational tool that allows the quantification of cell type and 299 
spatial LR interactions across time and space. We established a simulation -based ground-truth 300 
framework to measure and quantify its performance and demonstrated LARIS’s superior 301 
performance over existing methods. Applied to a human tonsil Slide -tags dataset, LARIS 302 
recovered canonical interactions underlying tissue organisation, cell migration, and immune 303 
responses, revealed previously unrecognised ligand sources, and separated cell states based on 304 
LR interaction patterns. In a Stereo -seq series of the developing mouse brain, LARIS resolved 305 
the spatial dynamics of LR interactions across cortical layers over multiple time points and linked 306 
these patterns to pathways central to brain development. 307 
 308 
Computational inferences of cell -cell interactions are powerful for hypothesis generation but 309 
ultimately require experimental validation to establish mechanism. Incorporating spatial context 310 
reduces predicted false positives; however, co -localisation (even physical proximity) does not 311 
ensure a functional effect on receiver cells because other mechanisms might mask or 312 
complement active signalling through parallel signals. A further limitation is that transcriptomics 313 
measures mRNA, whereas proteins (and their post -translational modifications) drive signalling. 314 
Coupling to proteomic assays and integrating chromatin accessibility (e.g., ATAC-seq) to read out 315 
responses in receiver cells will strengthen causal interpretation. 316 
 317 
Our benchmarking framework was designed to mimic real -world datasets and prioritise the 318 
reliable recovery of ligand-receptor (LR) pairs. A current limitation is that it does not directly assess 319

downstream consequences of LR interaction, such as the activation of subsequent signalling or 320 
ultimately transcriptional programs by the receptors in the receiver cell types. The LR interaction 321 
scores generated by LARIS, however, does provide a quantitative foundation to bridge this gap; 322 
these scores could be correlated with differential gene expression in the receiver cell types to link 323 
LR interaction changes with functional effects. Future simulation frameworks that explicitly model 324 
the propagation of signalling cascades and downstream transcriptional changes would provide 325 
an invaluable reference for robustly evaluating such downstream predictions. 326 
 327 
Many interactions involve co-receptors or multimeric ligands that act as complexes. LARIS does 328 
not yet model complex stoichiometry explicitly, which is an avenue for improvement. Given the 329 
zero-inflated nature of spatial assays, naively requiring all subunits to be co -detected would 330 
discard biologically plausible events lost to dropout and increase noise. Probabilistic complex 331 
scoring or partial-evidence models may offer a better balance between specificity and sensitivity. 332 
 333 
We have demonstrated that LARIS can comparatively analyse and quantify interactions across 334 
time points; it could likewise be used to contrast signalling between conditions and matched 335 
controls, enabling differential LR communication analyses. 336 
 337 
New spatial technologies are being developed constantly, and the field is moving towards the 338 
spatial profiling of cells compared to just dissociated single-cell data. LARIS will be an ideal tool 339 
to uncover and disentangle the hidden information inside the data and to point the most relevant 340 
focuses for future experimental planning. As the field moves towards better resolution and wider 341 
gene coverage, LARIS will likely be able to identify the most relevant ligand and receptors in the 342 
profiled sample and be ideal to analyse and quantify interactions across time and space. 343

Identification of niche enrichment of interactions 563 
To detect LR interactions that are enriched in functional regions or niches independent of cell 564 
type, we first assign regional labels to cells (e.g., cortical upper vs. deep layers). Because the LR 565 
integration score is defined per cell, standard single -cell differential frameworks can be applied 566 
directly: we compare per-cell LR scores across regions to identify interactions that are regionally 567 
differentially expressed. In practice, we treat each LR pair as a feature (gene) and perform 568 
differential testing across the region groups (e.g., marker -identification/rank-based tests with 569 
multiple-testing correction), potentially reporting effect sizes and region -wise prevalence. This 570 
yields a list of region -specific LR interactions that reflect spatially localized signaling programs 571 
without relying on cell type annotations; if desired, the same analysis can be repeated within cell 572 
type strata to differentiate regional effects per cell type. 573 
Benchmarking performance 574 
Simulation of scRNA-seq data 575 
The scRNA-seq data were simulated using a Python implementation of Splatter 10,11. To mimic a 576 
real biological dataset, we used the Tonsil dataset from the Slide-tags study as the reference and 577 
fit parameters with Splatter’s splatEstimate, thereby reproducing its dropout rates and expression 578 
distributions. We simulated the same number of genes as in the reference transcriptome (26,081) 579 
and varied the number of single -cells per simulation according to the associated spatial design. 580 
The number of cell types in each simulation was determined by the underlying spatial structure; 581 
within a simulation, some clusters were designed to exhibit more distinct differential -expression 582 
patterns than others. To avoid unnecessary complexity and potential confounders in 583 
benchmarking, we did not simulate batch effects or doublets. Full parameter and design details 584 
are provided in Supplementary Table 2. 585

Processing of simulated scRNA-seq data 587 
The simulated raw count matrices were then processed as if they were real data examples using 588 
Scanpy57. The total unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts were normalised to 10000 UMI per 589 
cell using the normalize_total function, then log-transformed with the log1p function, and the top 590 
2,000 highly variable genes were selected with highly_variable_genes. For visualization in two 591 
dimensions, we embedded the cells in a UMAP58 using the top 50 principal components, all other 592 
settings were left at default. Each cell was provided a cluster (cell type) label by the simulation. A 593 
simulation was considered successful when the cell types given by the simulation were clearly 594 
separated on the UMAP, and when the cell and gene quality metrics matched the tonsil reference 595 
(Extended Data Fig. 2). 596 
Spatial structure generation 597 
To generate spatial structures, we used two separate approaches. For the fully synthetic 598 
structures, scCube’s simulate_cluster and simulate_stripes functions were used12. The underlying 599 
structure was generated by specifying the shapes, centroids, and sizes of each region and by 600 
defining the total cell number to be simulated. The resulting cluster labels with spatial coordinates 601 
were then populated with the previously simulated single-cells to create the final spatial data used 602 
for benchmarking. For the structures mimicking real tissue examples, the hematoxylin and eosin 603 
(H&E) stained samples were manually segmented, separating regions showing different tissue 604 
architecture. The segmented regions were then processed in Python by assigning labels to each 605 
region, then merging regions based on perceived functionality and tissue morphology. In the final 606 
step, the tissue was populated by single -cells from the corresponding simulations. For the 607 
examples where H&E staining was not available, the structural schematics were used as the 608 
reference structure. 609

CellChat, CellChat spatial, and NICHES analysis 646 
All analyses were run according to the available tutorials. For the CellChat analysis the spatial 647 
count matrix was first normalized and log transformed. The spatial conversion factor was set to 648 
resemble real life examples with a maximum communication distance of 250 μm, and spot size 649 
of 1. The data were then processed using the functions identifyOverExpressedGenes and 650 
identifyOverExpressedInteractions with the default parameters. To infer the cluster -level 651 
interaction scores the computeCommunProb function was used with trim set to 0.1 in the 652 
”truncatedMean” mode. Interactions with less than 10 cells participating were removed with the 653 
filterCommunication function. All interactions were treated as ‘Secreted Signaling’. For the 654 
NICHES analysis the raw count matrices were SCTransform normalised using the version 5 655 
Seurat implementation59, PCA and UMAP were run afterwards using the RunPCA and RunUMAP 656 
functions using the top 30 principal components. Before running the prediction the data was 657 
imputed using RunALRA. The prediction was run using the RunNICHES function in the 658 
”CellToCellSpatial” mode with k=4. The final list of interactions was calculated between all 659 
possible cell types. The same LR interaction database was used to benchmark the performance 660 
of different methods. Interactions were ranked based on their interaction scores for LARIS, 661 
interaction probabilities for CellChat, and Wilcoxon test P values and average log2 fold changes 662 
for NICHES. 663

Measure performance 664 
To assess the capability of different methods to recover the highest -ranked (and deemed most 665 
relevant) interactions in the cluster-level ground truth, we compared the recovery “speed” of each 666 
method for the first 100 interactions in the ground truth against the top 1,000 interactions in each 667 
method and then calculated the area under the curve (AUC). The proportion of recovered 668 
interactions among the top 1,000 ground-truth interactions was calculated by comparing the top 669 
1,000 prediction outputs against the ground truth. To quantify the false -positive rate of the 670 
methods, we calculated the rate of interactions between spatially non-proximal clusters, meaning 671 
that communication would have been physically hindered in a real-life scenario. 672

embedded the cells with UMAP using the top 50 principal components; all other parameters were 713 
left at their defaults. Cell type annotations were transferred from the original work 2. The cluster 714 
annotated as myeloid cells was reassigned as macrophages, and FDCs were split and annotated 715 
as either FDCs or MRCs based on known marker genes. 716 
Stereo-seq mouse brain data 717 
The Stereo-seq mouse samples were processed with Scanpy57. The original binning of the beads 718 
was kept. Whole embryo slices were cropped to keep only the brain. Cells with fewer than 100 719 
detected genes were removed using filter_cells, and genes expressed in fewer than 3 cells were 720 
removed using filter_genes. Raw UMI counts were normalized to 10,000 UMI per cell using 721 
normalize_total, then log -transformed with log1p. The leiden function was used to cluster the 722 
binned cells, and the resulting clusters were annotated as in the original works according to their 723 
anatomical regions. If the original annotation was available it was kept, leiden resolution was 724 
chosen to achieve clear separation. Upper and deep layers were separated according to the 725 
clustering based on known layer specific markers. 726 
Analysis with LARIS 727 
Slide-tags human tonsil data 728 
To calculate the integrated LR scores for each cell, we applied the prepareLRInteraction function 729 
from LARIS (number_nearest_neighbors=20). Interactions with spatial specificity and variability, 730 
relative to randomly shuffled locations, were identified using the runLARIS function 731 
(n_nearest_neighbors=20, mu=0.25, n_repeats=5, sigma=100). To infer and rank interactions at 732 
the cluster level, we employed the _calculate_laris_score_by_celltype function (mu=100, 733 
mask_threshold=1e-6) within the runLARIS function. To cluster B germinal centre cells by their 734 
interactions, we first filtered the cluster -level predictions to the top 3,000 highest -ranked 735 
interactions and selected those LR pairs in which B germinal centre cells were either senders or 736 
receivers, yielding a total of 161 interactions. The B germinal centre cells were then subset, their 737 
LR scores log-transformed, and PCA and UMAP were constructed on the LR scores with default 738 
parameters. The leiden function was used to cluster the cells (resolution=1.1), and the resulting 739 
clusters were assigned to dark or light zones based on known marker genes. To visualize the DZ 740 
(‘CXCR4’, ‘AICDA’, ‘FOXP1’, ‘MME’) and LZ (‘CD83’, ‘LMO2’, ‘BCL2A1’) genes as modules, we 741 
used the score_genes function. Regionally enriched interactions were identified with COSG 742 
(mu=100, expressed_pct=0.15, remove_lowly_expressed=True, n_genes_user=100) 61. To 743

"""End-to-end integration test based on the LARIS tutorial.

Uses the tonsil dataset (5,695 cells x 25,583 genes, 14 cell types) and
the bundled CellChatDB human database to run the full LARIS pipeline:

    load data → prepareLRInteraction → runLARIS → plotting functions

This mirrors the official tutorial at:
    https://genecell.github.io/LARIS/notebooks/04_LARIS_tutorial.html

Data location (checked in order):
    1. $LARIS_TEST_DATA environment variable (path to directory containing
       adata_tonsil.h5ad)
    2. Default: tests/data/ relative to the repo root

Set the environment variable to point at your local copy, e.g.:
    export LARIS_TEST_DATA=/data1/mdai/Result/single-cell/Methods/LARIS/tutorial

import warnings

class TestRunLARIS:

        for col in ["ligand", "receptor", "score", "Rank"]:
            assert col in laris_lr.columns

    def test_laris_lr_sorted_descending(self, laris_lr):
        scores = laris_lr["score"].values
        assert np.all(scores[:-1] >= scores[1:])

    def test_res_LARIS_is_dataframe(self, res_LARIS):
        assert isinstance(res_LARIS, pd.DataFrame)

    def test_res_LARIS_has_expected_columns(self, res_LARIS):
        expected = [
            "sender", "receiver", "ligand", "receptor",
            "interaction_name", "interaction_score",
            "p_value", "p_value_fdr", "nlog10_p_value_fdr",
        ]
        for col in expected:
            assert col in res_LARIS.columns, f"Missing column: {col}"

    def test_res_LARIS_nonempty(self, res_LARIS):
        assert len(res_LARIS) > 0

        for col in ["p_value", "p_value_fdr"]:
            vals = res_LARIS[col].dropna()
            assert (vals >= 0).all(), f"{col} has negative values"
            assert (vals <= 1).all(), f"{col} has values > 1"

    def test_significant_interactions_exist(self, res_LARIS):
        n_sig = (res_LARIS["p_value_fdr"] < 0.05).sum()
        assert n_sig > 0, "Expected some significant interactions"

    def test_pvalue_diversity(self, res_LARIS):
        """After dedup fix, p-values should not be massively duplicated."""
        pvals = res_LARIS["p_value"].dropna().values
        nontrivial = pvals[pvals < 1.0]
        n_unique = len(np.unique(nontrivial))
        assert n_unique > 50, (
            f"Only {n_unique} distinct non-trivial p-values — "
            "possible regression of dedup fix"
        )

    def test_all_cell_types_present(self, res_LARIS, adata):
        senders = set(res_LARIS["sender"].unique())
        receivers = set(res_LARIS["receiver"].unique())
        cell_types = set(adata.obs["cell_type"].unique())
        # Not all cell types need to appear, but most should
        assert len(senders & cell_types) >= 10
        assert len(receivers & cell_types) >= 10

        for name in res_LARIS["interaction_name"].head(20):
            assert "::" in name

        n_total = len(res_LARIS)
        n_dedup = res_LARIS.drop_duplicates().shape[0]
        assert n_total == n_dedup

class TestSpatialOffsetRealData:
    """Test spatialOffsetMultisample on the tonsil data split into pseudo-samples."""

    def test_pseudo_multisample(self, adata):
        """Split tonsil into 2 pseudo-samples and verify offset works."""
        import anndata as ad

        adata_copy = adata.copy()
        n = adata_copy.n_obs
        adata_copy.obs["pseudo_sample"] = (
            ["sampleA"] * (n // 2) + ["sampleB"] * (n - n // 2)
        )

        la.pp.spatialOffsetMultisample(
            adata_copy,
            sampleKey="pseudo_sample",
            spatialKey="X_spatial",
        )

        assert "spatial_offset_info" in adata_copy.uns
        info = adata_copy.uns["spatial_offset_info"]
        assert set(info["samples"].keys()) == {"sampleA", "sampleB"}

"""
LARIS Datasets Module (laris.datasets)

Provides bundled ligand-receptor interaction databases for convenient access.

Available databases:
- CellChatDB human: 2,951 curated ligand-receptor pairs
- CellChatDB mouse: 3,105 curated ligand-receptor pairs

Example usage:
    >>> import laris as la
    >>> lr_df = la.datasets.lrDatabase('human')
    >>> lr_df.shape
    (2951, 28)
    >>> lr_df_signaling = la.datasets.lrDatabase('human', pathway='WNT')
"""

import importlib.resources
import pandas as pd


def lrDatabase(species='human', pathway=None, annotation=None):
    """Load a bundled ligand-receptor interaction database.

    Parameters
    ----------
    species : str, default 'human'
        Species for the database. One of 'human' or 'mouse'.
    pathway : str, optional
        Filter to a specific signaling pathway (e.g., 'WNT', 'TGFb').
        Matches the ``pathway_name`` column. Case-sensitive.
    annotation : str, optional
        Filter to a specific annotation category (e.g., 'Secreted Signaling',
        'ECM-Receptor', 'Cell-Cell Contact'). Matches the ``annotation``
        column. Case-sensitive.

    Returns
    -------
    pd.DataFrame
        Ligand-receptor database with columns including ``interaction_name``,
        ``pathway_name``, ``ligand``, ``receptor``, ``annotation``, etc.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``species`` is not 'human' or 'mouse'.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import laris as la
    >>> lr_human = la.datasets.lrDatabase('human')
    >>> lr_mouse = la.datasets.lrDatabase('mouse')
    >>> lr_wnt = la.datasets.lrDatabase('human', pathway='WNT')
    """
    species = species.lower()
    _files = {
        'human': 'human_lr_CellChatDB.csv',
        'mouse': 'mouse_lr_CellChatDB.csv',
    }

    if species not in _files:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unknown species '{species}'. Choose from: {list(_files.keys())}"
        )

    data_dir = importlib.resources.files(__package__) / '_data'
    csv_path = data_dir / _files[species]

    with importlib.resources.as_file(csv_path) as path:
        df = pd.read_csv(path)

    if pathway is not None:
        df = df[df['pathway_name'] == pathway].reset_index(drop=True)

    if annotation is not None:
        df = df[df['annotation'] == annotation].reset_index(drop=True)

    return df


__all__ = ['lrDatabase']

Abstract 15 
Advances in spatially resolved transcriptomics provide unprecedented opportunities to 16 
characterise intercellular communication pathways. However, robust and computationally efficient 17 
incorporation of spatial information into intercellular communication inference remains 18 
challenging. Here, we present LARIS ( Ligand And Receptor Interaction analysis in Spatial 19 
transcriptomics), an accurate and scalable method that identifies cell type -specific and spatially 20 
restricted ligand-receptor (LR) interactions at single-cell or bead resolution. LARIS is compatible 21 
with all spatial transcriptomic technologies and quantifies specificity, infers sender -receiver 22 
directionality, and detects how differential interactions vary across time and space. To compare 23 
LARIS with existing methods, we established a simulation framework to generate ground truth of 24 
LR interactions with defined tissue architecture and gene expression patterns. LARIS 25 
demonstrates superior performances over other methods in accuracy and scalability. We further 26 
applied LARIS to human tonsil and developing mouse cortex spatial transcriptomics datasets 27 
collected from various spatial techniques. This uncovered the signalling mechanisms shaping 28 
tissue organisation and their changes over time. LARIS reveals cell type-, niche-, and condition-29 
specific signalling and scales to hundreds of thousands of cells in minutes. This provides an 30 
efficient and direct method for discovering the molecular interplay between apposed cells across 31 
development. 32 
Introduction 33 
Intercellular communication orchestrates tissue development, homeostasis, and responses to 34 
stress and disease 1. Computational inference of ligand -receptor (LR) interactions from 35 
transcriptomic data has therefore become a cornerstone for charting cellular interactions in 36 
complex tissues. However, computationally inference of cell -cell communication (CCC) faces 37 
challenges, including data sparsity, and spatial heterogeneity. Although recent advances in CCC 38 
algorithms have attempted to address some of these challenges by gene expression imputation 39 
and incorporating spatial constraints on LR interactions at populational level, they still struggle 40 
with low sensitivity and specificity, missing relevant interactions, producing many false -positive 41 
hits, respectively. Thus, sensitive, spatially resolved, and single -cell level reconstruction of 42 
intercellular communication networks remains a major unmet need1.  43 
 44 
To meet these needs, we introduce LARIS ( Ligand And Receptor Interaction analysis in Spatial 45 
transcriptomics) as an accurate method for LR interaction and CCC inference in spatial 46 
transcriptomic data. LARIS enhances the spatial interaction detection by combining in silico LR 47 
diffusion and local cellular heterogeneity via a spatial k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) graph, to infer 48 
single-cell level LR interaction scores and spatial specific CCC with cosine similarity. To rigorously 49 
compare our success with previous efforts, we also establish a spatial transcriptomics simulation 50 
framework that provides a reference ground truth for benchmarking CCC methods. We show that 51 
LARIS outperforms existing methods, accurately recovering spatial and cell type -specific 52 
interactions while maintaining low spatial false -positive rates. We further demonstrate the 53 
capabilities of LARIS in two case studies: (i) a human tonsil Slide -tags dataset2, where LARIS 54 
resolves niche - and cell -state-specific communication and recovers both known and novel 55 
signals; and (ii) a developing mouse cerebral cortex Stereo-seq dataset3–5, where LARIS identifies 56

layer-specific interactions and quantifies their temporal dynamics during development. Taken 57 
together, LARIS provides an accurate, scalable, and adaptable framework to infer ligand and 58 
receptor dynamics and decipher intercellular communication in complex biological systems. 59 
 60 
Results 61 
 62 
Overview of LARIS 63 
LARIS is designed to identify and characterize LR interactions from spatial transcriptomics data 64 
using known databases and is compatible with both single -cell and bead/spot -based spatial 65 
datasets, enabling the discovery of cellular communication across diverse platforms (Fig. 1a and 66 
Extended Data Fig. 1). To improve both sensitivity and specificity, LARIS uses interaction 67 
abundance and cosine similarity to identify biologically relevant interactions, and a spatial k-NN 68 
graph to ensure that only spatially proximal cells are identified as interacting. 69 
 70 
LARIS begins by constructing a k-NN graph weighted by the physical distance between cells or 71 
spots (Fig. 1b). Using this spatial graph, the normalized ligand and receptor expression values 72 
are spatially diffused, modelling the local availability of each (Fig. 1c). An LR interaction score is 73 
then calculated for each cell or spot by element -wise product (i.e., Hadamard product) of the 74 
diffused ligand and receptor expression (Fig. 1d). To prevent diffusion artifacts from generating 75 
false-positive interactions, this score is set to zero if the cell or spot did not express either the 76 
ligand or the receptor in the original gene expression data. This scoring at the individual -cell or 77 
spot level increases sensitivity for interactions involving rare cell types and reveals communication 78 
patterns within subpopulations that are otherwise obscured by cluster -level or aggregated 79 
methods (e.g., CellChat6 and CellPhoneDB7). 80 
 81 
Building on these LR scores at single-cell/spot resolution, LARIS provides three complementary 82 
analytic approaches to discover the most specific interactions. First, LARIS identifies LR 83 
interactions with strong spatial patterns (Fig. 1e) using a cell type -agonistic approach. LARIS 84 
computes the cosine similarity between the calculated LR interaction scores and a spatially 85 
diffused version of those same scores. Building on the idea of negative sampling in network 86 
representation learning8, this observed similarity score is then corrected against a null value 87 
derived from spatially shuffled data. This yields a final spatial -specificity score for each LR pair 88 
(see Methods), of which the higher value indicates a stronger spatially localized pattern. 89 
 90 
Second, LARIS infers communication directionality between sender and receiver cell types (Fig. 91 
1f). To achieve this, it quantifies: (i) the cell-type specificity of ligand and receptor expression, (ii) 92 
the abundance of each LR pair for every cell type pairing, and (iii) a neighbourhood-enrichment 93 
score to detect co-localizing interactions between cell types. Combining this information with the 94 
LR spatial-specificity score yields a score for each LR pair in each sender-receiver cell type pair, 95 
which enables further prioritization of LR interactions based on cell types of interest and analysis 96 
of cell type communication patterns. 97 
 98 
Third, LARIS identifies differentially active interactions among different conditions or contexts, 99 
such as predefined tissue regions/niches, developmental stages or disease progressions (Fig. 100

1g). LARIS facilitates statistical testing on the single -cell/spot level LR interaction score to 101 
discover LR pairs significantly enriched or depleted in one condition or context compared to 102 
another (see Methods). 103 
 104 
The single-cell/spot level quantification of LR interaction strength, coupled with the three -views 105 
interpretation, i.e., spatial specificity, cell type directionality and differential interaction among 106 
conditions, enables LARIS to be an efficient and accurate method for characterizing the LR 107 
interaction and cell-cell communication dynamics. 108 
 109 
Benchmarking on simulated data 110 
 111 
Prior work has highlighted low concordance among CCC methods, with major differences in top-112 
ranked predictions9. These discrepancies stem from divergent LR databases, the inclusion of 113 
interactions lacking experimental validation, and distinct model architectures 1,9. A persistent 114 
challenge in the field has been the benchmarking of these tools, which is hampered by the 115 
absence of comprehensive experimentally validated ground-truth datasets. 116 
 117 
To address this gap, we designed a simulation framework to generate spatial transcriptomics data 118 
with real-world tissue characteristics and known ground-truth LR interactions, providing full control 119 
over cell locations, gene expression (including genes that encode ligands and receptors), and 120 
active LR pairs with different levels of spatial and cell type specificities (Fig. 2a). This methodology 121 
enables rigorous, quantitative performance comparisons. 122 
 123 
The workflow first simulates scRNA -seq data using Splatter 10,11. Simulation parameters were 124 
calibrated to ensure that cell type identities are distinct and that quality metrics—such as dropout 125 
rates, unique molecule identifier (UMI) distributions, and gene variance —closely mimic those of 126 
a real-world reference, a human tonsil Slide -tags single nuclei RNA -seq dataset2 (Fig. 2b and 127 
Extended Data Fig.2). Next, these simulated cells are mapped onto complex spatial structures, 128 
which are generated either de novo using scCube12 or by templating from real tissue architectures, 129 
including mouse lung, small intestine, and developing brainstem, hair follicle and lymph node (Fig. 130 
2c, d). 131 
 132 
To establish a ranked ground truth, we defined an interaction's importance based on its 133 
expression specificity and spatial likelihood. First, we computed a 'relevance score' for each ligand 134 
and receptor in different cell types based on the simulation parameters that account for its 135 
simulated expression abundance and cell -type specificity (Extended Data Fig.3; see Methods). 136 
The ground -truth LR interaction ranking was then generated by multiplying these ligand and 137 
receptor relevance scores across all cell-type pairings. This comprehensive list was subsequently 138 
filtered for spatial feasibility, resulting in a final, ranked set of active LR interactions with varying 139 
specificities, known to occur between spatially proximal cell types (Fig. 2e, f). 140 
 141 
Using this ground-truth simulation framework, we compared LARIS against other CCC methods, 142 
including CellChat (non-spatial)13, CellChat-spatial (v2)6, and NICHES14. First, we assessed the 143 
efficiency of each method in prioritizing the top ranked ground -truth LR interactions. We plotted 144

recovery curves, showing the number of top ground -truth hits recovered as a function of 145 
increasing prediction rank (Fig. 2h and Methods). LARIS demonstrated a higher area under the 146 
curve, indicating it successfully ranked the most critical ground -truth interactions higher than all 147 
other methods (Supplementary Table 1). The non -spatial and spatial versions of CellChat 148 
performed similarly, while NICHES recovered substantially fewer of these high -priority 149 
interactions. We next evaluated the overall recall by calculating the proportion of ground -truth 150 
interactions recovered within the top 1,000 predictions of each method (Fig. 2h). LARIS again 151 
performed best, and CellChat -spatial outperformed the original CellChat, confirming that the 152 
incorporation of spatial information improves discovery. Finally, we evaluated the spatial false -153 
positive rate, defined as the proportion of predicted interactions occurring between cell types that 154 
were not spatially proximal in the simulation. LARIS and NICHES both exhibited very low false -155 
positive rates (Fig. 2i). In contrast, CellChat performed worst, with over 40% of its predictions 156 
being spatially false positives, highlighting the critical advantage of integrating spatial information 157 
for CCC inference. 158 
 159 
Taken together, our spatial simulation framework provides a unified and unbiased approach for 160 
benchmarking CCC methods’ performance on spatial transcriptomics data. Across all metrics, 161 
LARIS outperformed existing methods, demonstrating superior recovery of spatial and cell type-162 
specific, high -priority interactions while maintaining a low spatial false -positive rate, thereby 163 
validating the efficacy of our approach. 164 
 165 
LARIS identifies ligand -receptor interactions defining zonations of germinal centres in 166 
human tonsil 167 
 168 
We next tested LARIS’s ability to profile cellular communications on the human tonsil Slide -tags 169 
dataset2, as this enables us to assess/quantify LR dynamics at single-nucleus resolution within a 170 
tissue with well-characterised spatial structures and LR interactions, offering a robust reference 171 
for benchmarking (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a)15.  172 
 173 
First, we asked whether LR scores alone could distinguish dark- and light-zone identity in germinal 174 
centre (GC) B cells, a task that is challenging with scRNA-seq. The dark zone hosts proliferating 175 
B cells undergoing somatic hypermutation; the light zone mediates affinity -based selection via 176 
follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells15. De novo clustering of LR scores 177 
separated GC B cells (Fig. 3b and  Extended Data Fig. 4b), a pattern validated by the expression 178 
of canonical dark zone and light zone gene modules16 (Fig. 3c). Zone-specific enrichment analysis 179 
revealed distinct communication programs: BMP7 and its receptors interact in the dark zone; 180 
BMP7 signalling has been reported to induce apoptosis and negatively regulate GC B -cell 181 
survival17,18. In contrast, L21-IL21R interactions, characteristic of Tfh -derived signalling, were 182 
enriched in the light zone, supporting the role of IL21 in promoting GC B-cell expansion and early 183 
plasma cell differentiation19,20 (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4c, d). 184 
 185 
LARIS identifies marginal reticular cells as key signalling hubs in human tonsil 186 
 187

(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made

Reclustering using the LR scores combined with gene expression separated FDCs from marginal 188 
reticular cells (MRCs), revealing two distinct signalling patterns of cell populations within the 189 
originally annotated FDCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e). The identities of FDCs and MRCs were 190 
validated using canonical marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 4f)21, and spatial mapping confirmed 191 
their respective localization, with FDCs restricted to germinal centres and MRCs positioned in the 192 
surrounding regions (Fig. 3d). 193 
 194 
To further characterise regional niches, we computed neighbourhood enrichment scores for each 195 
cell type (Fig. 3e). Unsupervised clustering on cell neighbourhood enrichment has clearly 196 
separated the germinal centres, B, and T cell rich zones. FDCs primarily communicate with 197 
germinal-centre cells, including Tfh and GC B, and plasma cells, whereas MRCs interact more 198 
broadly with naïve and memory B cells as well as pDC, mDC, and multiple T -cell subsets. 199 
Interestingly, macrophages showed no strong enrichment in any of those regions, contributing to 200 
regulation in all regions of the tonsil22.  201 
 202 
While FDCs and MRCs occupy distinct niches and differ in their interacting partners, they 203 
converge in specific signalling programs. Both express C3, a key complement component 204 
involved in antigen presentation23,24 (Fig. 3f), and MRCs additionally produce soluble regulators 205 
of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways25–28 (Extended Data Fig. 4j). 206 
 207 
We also discovered distinct LR interactions associated with FDCs and MRCs: Inside the germinal 208 
centres, FDCs and macrophages express the checkpoint ligands PD -L1 (CD274) and PD -L2 209 
(PDCD1LG2), positioning them to modulate Tfh cells through PD -1 (PDCD1) 29. FDCs also 210 
uniquely express WNT5A, which supports germinal-centre B-cell survival via non-canonical WNT 211 
signalling30; in our data, we identified FZD3 as the likely interacting partner. Interestingly, we found 212 
that GC B cells express high levels of PDGFD, which could influence the clonal expansion and 213 
differentiation of the PDGFRβ positive MRCs into FDCs31–34 (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). 214 
 215 
Outside the germinal centres, MRCs express TNFSF13B (BAFF), often considered a defining 216 
FDC product35,36. We found that FDCs within the germinal centres express very low levels (Fig. 217 
3e), consistent with flow cytometry and scRNA -seq data21. TNFSF13B is an essential survival 218 
factor for naïve B cells 35, although it is dispensable for germinal -centre B-cell survival37. In our 219 
dataset, macrophages and mDCs were also substantial sources of TNFSF13B, supporting their 220 
contribution to B -cell survival and differentiation. Lack of TNFSF13B leads to failure of FDC 221 
maturation; consequently, stimulation of B cells via immune complexes can not occur 38. Beyond 222 
their effects on B cells, MRCs help organise T cell -rich zones in the paracortex by secreting 223 
CCL19 and CCL21, chemokines that recruit CCR7-positive cells39, including T cells, NK cells, and 224 
mDCs in the tonsil. MRCs supply CSF1 and IL34 which are important growth factors required for 225 
the control of monocyte and macrophage differentiation, survival, proliferation, and renewal 40, 226 
suggesting their importance in macrophage development and differentiation outside of germinal 227 
centres. These findings highlight the importance of MRCs as tissue organisers in tonsil that signal 228 
to B cells, T cells, and macrophages shaping their  development, survival, and migration 229 
(Extended Data Fig.  4i). 230

analysis of LR interactions between the two populations. The Gene Ontology (GO) analysis 233 
revealed both shared and distinct biological processes (Fig. 3h)41: For example, GO terms related 234 
to dendritic cell antigen processing and presentation were significantly enriched in MRCs, 235 
whereas the ERBB2 signalling pathway was enriched in FDCs. 236 
 237 
By applying LARIS to a human tonsil Slide -tags sample, we demonstrated that it can resolve 238 
distinct cell states within a cell type and identify the LR interactions enriched for those states. Its 239 
single-cell level scoring further guided the analysis by revealing spatially distinct communication 240 
patterns of FDCs and MRCs. LARIS recovered known LR pairs and connected them to sender 241 
and receiver cell types in the tonsil and suggested previously uncharacterised communications 242 
that influence cell survival, migration, and maturation. 243 
 244 
LARIS identifies region and time specific interactions in the developing mouse brain 245 
 246 
We next applied LARIS to map the spatiotemporal dynamics of LR interactions during mouse 247 
brain development, a process governed by spatially organized signalling cascades42. We focused 248 
on the cerebral cortex, a structure defined by its distinct layered architecture and corresponding 249 
functional and transcriptional heterogeneity43. 250 
 251 
To assess this we applied LARIS to Stereo -seq datasets collected at different developmental 252 
stages of the mouse brain, i.e., embryonic day (E)14.5, E16.5, postnatal day (P)7, P14, and P773–253 
5 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). We annotated the cortex as upper and deep layers for the 254 
postnatal samples, and for the prenatal samples we included additional developmental cell types 255 
(Fig. 4a). 256 
 257 
LARIS identified differentially enriched spatial LR interactions across mouse cortex development. 258 
For example, the Slit1::Robo1 interaction, known to modulates proliferation and neurogenesis44,45, 259 
axon guidance and neuronal migration 46,47, was restricted to upper layer neurons prenatally but 260 
present in both upper and deep layer postnatally (Fig. 4b). Another intriguing example, the 261 
Sema3c::Plxna4 interaction, which was most prominent in the migrating and deep layer neurons 262 
prenatally, yet only sporadically present in the postnatal cortex (Fig. 4b). Sema3a, a closely 263 
related ligand with similar structure and expression to Sema3c, regulates interneuron positioning 264 
via Plxna448. By contrast, the role of Sema3c in the developing mouse cortex remains unknown, 265 
raising the possibility of a Sema3c::Plxna4 signalling axis. 266 
 267 
To systematically analyse the LR interactions identified by LARIS, we grouped them by function 268 
(e.g., neurotransmitters, axon guidance, growth modulators, Wnt signalling) and plotted their 269 
strengths across developmental stages and cortical layers (Fig. 4c). This revealed clear stage -270 
specific activities patterns of different ligand -receptor pairs. For example, among the growth 271 
modulators, Igf2::Igfr2 49, Fgf15::Fgfr2 50, Mdk::Sdc1 51, Dlk1::Notch2 52, Jag1::Notch 53 were 272 
primarily enriched prenatally In contrast, Fgf1::Fgfr1, Fgf9::Fgfr1, Fgf20::Fgfr2, were predominant 273 
in the adult brain, likely contributing to neuronal maintenance54,55. 274

To connect these LR interactions to underlying biological processes, we performed Gene Set 276 
Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)41 on the differentially expressed LR pairs at different stages (Fig. 277 
4d). The results confirmed expected developmental trajectories: prenatal stages were enriched 278 
for gene function terms such as 'axon guidance', while the adult stage was dominated by 279 
pathways related to synaptic integration (e.g., 'neuroactive ligand -receptor interaction', 280 
'glutamatergic synapse', 'GABAergic synapse', and 'synaptic vesicle cycle').  281 
 282 
We also examined LR interactions along specific spatial axes. Along the dorsal -ventral axis, 283 
Slit1:Robo1, Efnb1::Epha4, and Lrfn5::Ptprs showed clear spatiotemporal dynamics (Fig. 4d). 284 
Along the rostral -caudal axis, we further identified multiple spatially restricted interactions 285 
(Extended Data Fig. 5b, c). For example, Aldh1a3, which encodes an enzyme that converts 286 
retinaldehyde into retinoic acid, was expressed at P7 specially in the caudal upper layer 287 
corresponding to the forming visual area. This pattern was confirmed by Allen Institute’s in situ 288 
hybridization (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Other examples include Cdh12:Itgb1 enrichment in the 289 
rostral cortex and Penk, an opioid polypeptide hormone, enrichment in the rostral deep layers 290 
postnatally (Extended Data Fig. 5b, c). 291 
 292 
Together, these spatiotemporal analyses on mouse cortex development demonstrated that 293 
LARIS can identify and characterise key signalling molecules and pathways underlying the 294 
complex intracellular and intercellular dynamics through development. 295 
 296 
Discussion 297 
 298 
Here we presented LARIS, a computational tool that allows the quantification of cell type and 299 
spatial LR interactions across time and space. We established a simulation -based ground-truth 300 
framework to measure and quantify its performance and demonstrated LARIS’s superior 301 
performance over existing methods. Applied to a human tonsil Slide -tags dataset, LARIS 302 
recovered canonical interactions underlying tissue organisation, cell migration, and immune 303 
responses, revealed previously unrecognised ligand sources, and separated cell states based on 304 
LR interaction patterns. In a Stereo -seq series of the developing mouse brain, LARIS resolved 305 
the spatial dynamics of LR interactions across cortical layers over multiple time points and linked 306 
these patterns to pathways central to brain development. 307 
 308 
Computational inferences of cell -cell interactions are powerful for hypothesis generation but 309 
ultimately require experimental validation to establish mechanism. Incorporating spatial context 310 
reduces predicted false positives; however, co -localisation (even physical proximity) does not 311 
ensure a functional effect on receiver cells because other mechanisms might mask or 312 
complement active signalling through parallel signals. A further limitation is that transcriptomics 313 
measures mRNA, whereas proteins (and their post -translational modifications) drive signalling. 314 
Coupling to proteomic assays and integrating chromatin accessibility (e.g., ATAC-seq) to read out 315 
responses in receiver cells will strengthen causal interpretation. 316 
 317 
Our benchmarking framework was designed to mimic real -world datasets and prioritise the 318 
reliable recovery of ligand-receptor (LR) pairs. A current limitation is that it does not directly assess 319

downstream consequences of LR interaction, such as the activation of subsequent signalling or 320 
ultimately transcriptional programs by the receptors in the receiver cell types. The LR interaction 321 
scores generated by LARIS, however, does provide a quantitative foundation to bridge this gap; 322 
these scores could be correlated with differential gene expression in the receiver cell types to link 323 
LR interaction changes with functional effects. Future simulation frameworks that explicitly model 324 
the propagation of signalling cascades and downstream transcriptional changes would provide 325 
an invaluable reference for robustly evaluating such downstream predictions. 326 
 327 
Many interactions involve co-receptors or multimeric ligands that act as complexes. LARIS does 328 
not yet model complex stoichiometry explicitly, which is an avenue for improvement. Given the 329 
zero-inflated nature of spatial assays, naively requiring all subunits to be co -detected would 330 
discard biologically plausible events lost to dropout and increase noise. Probabilistic complex 331 
scoring or partial-evidence models may offer a better balance between specificity and sensitivity. 332 
 333 
We have demonstrated that LARIS can comparatively analyse and quantify interactions across 334 
time points; it could likewise be used to contrast signalling between conditions and matched 335 
controls, enabling differential LR communication analyses. 336 
 337 
New spatial technologies are being developed constantly, and the field is moving towards the 338 
spatial profiling of cells compared to just dissociated single-cell data. LARIS will be an ideal tool 339 
to uncover and disentangle the hidden information inside the data and to point the most relevant 340 
focuses for future experimental planning. As the field moves towards better resolution and wider 341 
gene coverage, LARIS will likely be able to identify the most relevant ligand and receptors in the 342 
profiled sample and be ideal to analyse and quantify interactions across time and space. 343

Identification of niche enrichment of interactions 563 
To detect LR interactions that are enriched in functional regions or niches independent of cell 564 
type, we first assign regional labels to cells (e.g., cortical upper vs. deep layers). Because the LR 565 
integration score is defined per cell, standard single -cell differential frameworks can be applied 566 
directly: we compare per-cell LR scores across regions to identify interactions that are regionally 567 
differentially expressed. In practice, we treat each LR pair as a feature (gene) and perform 568 
differential testing across the region groups (e.g., marker -identification/rank-based tests with 569 
multiple-testing correction), potentially reporting effect sizes and region -wise prevalence. This 570 
yields a list of region -specific LR interactions that reflect spatially localized signaling programs 571 
without relying on cell type annotations; if desired, the same analysis can be repeated within cell 572 
type strata to differentiate regional effects per cell type. 573 
Benchmarking performance 574 
Simulation of scRNA-seq data 575 
The scRNA-seq data were simulated using a Python implementation of Splatter 10,11. To mimic a 576 
real biological dataset, we used the Tonsil dataset from the Slide-tags study as the reference and 577 
fit parameters with Splatter’s splatEstimate, thereby reproducing its dropout rates and expression 578 
distributions. We simulated the same number of genes as in the reference transcriptome (26,081) 579 
and varied the number of single -cells per simulation according to the associated spatial design. 580 
The number of cell types in each simulation was determined by the underlying spatial structure; 581 
within a simulation, some clusters were designed to exhibit more distinct differential -expression 582 
patterns than others. To avoid unnecessary complexity and potential confounders in 583 
benchmarking, we did not simulate batch effects or doublets. Full parameter and design details 584 
are provided in Supplementary Table 2. 585

Processing of simulated scRNA-seq data 587 
The simulated raw count matrices were then processed as if they were real data examples using 588 
Scanpy57. The total unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts were normalised to 10000 UMI per 589 
cell using the normalize_total function, then log-transformed with the log1p function, and the top 590 
2,000 highly variable genes were selected with highly_variable_genes. For visualization in two 591 
dimensions, we embedded the cells in a UMAP58 using the top 50 principal components, all other 592 
settings were left at default. Each cell was provided a cluster (cell type) label by the simulation. A 593 
simulation was considered successful when the cell types given by the simulation were clearly 594 
separated on the UMAP, and when the cell and gene quality metrics matched the tonsil reference 595 
(Extended Data Fig. 2). 596 
Spatial structure generation 597 
To generate spatial structures, we used two separate approaches. For the fully synthetic 598 
structures, scCube’s simulate_cluster and simulate_stripes functions were used12. The underlying 599 
structure was generated by specifying the shapes, centroids, and sizes of each region and by 600 
defining the total cell number to be simulated. The resulting cluster labels with spatial coordinates 601 
were then populated with the previously simulated single-cells to create the final spatial data used 602 
for benchmarking. For the structures mimicking real tissue examples, the hematoxylin and eosin 603 
(H&E) stained samples were manually segmented, separating regions showing different tissue 604 
architecture. The segmented regions were then processed in Python by assigning labels to each 605 
region, then merging regions based on perceived functionality and tissue morphology. In the final 606 
step, the tissue was populated by single -cells from the corresponding simulations. For the 607 
examples where H&E staining was not available, the structural schematics were used as the 608 
reference structure. 609

CellChat, CellChat spatial, and NICHES analysis 646 
All analyses were run according to the available tutorials. For the CellChat analysis the spatial 647 
count matrix was first normalized and log transformed. The spatial conversion factor was set to 648 
resemble real life examples with a maximum communication distance of 250 μm, and spot size 649 
of 1. The data were then processed using the functions identifyOverExpressedGenes and 650 
identifyOverExpressedInteractions with the default parameters. To infer the cluster -level 651 
interaction scores the computeCommunProb function was used with trim set to 0.1 in the 652 
”truncatedMean” mode. Interactions with less than 10 cells participating were removed with the 653 
filterCommunication function. All interactions were treated as ‘Secreted Signaling’. For the 654 
NICHES analysis the raw count matrices were SCTransform normalised using the version 5 655 
Seurat implementation59, PCA and UMAP were run afterwards using the RunPCA and RunUMAP 656 
functions using the top 30 principal components. Before running the prediction the data was 657 
imputed using RunALRA. The prediction was run using the RunNICHES function in the 658 
”CellToCellSpatial” mode with k=4. The final list of interactions was calculated between all 659 
possible cell types. The same LR interaction database was used to benchmark the performance 660 
of different methods. Interactions were ranked based on their interaction scores for LARIS, 661 
interaction probabilities for CellChat, and Wilcoxon test P values and average log2 fold changes 662 
for NICHES. 663

Measure performance 664 
To assess the capability of different methods to recover the highest -ranked (and deemed most 665 
relevant) interactions in the cluster-level ground truth, we compared the recovery “speed” of each 666 
method for the first 100 interactions in the ground truth against the top 1,000 interactions in each 667 
method and then calculated the area under the curve (AUC). The proportion of recovered 668 
interactions among the top 1,000 ground-truth interactions was calculated by comparing the top 669 
1,000 prediction outputs against the ground truth. To quantify the false -positive rate of the 670 
methods, we calculated the rate of interactions between spatially non-proximal clusters, meaning 671 
that communication would have been physically hindered in a real-life scenario. 672

Data processing 705 
Slide-tags human tonsil data 706 
The Slide-tags human tonsil dataset was reprocessed with Scanpy 57. Cells with fewer than 100 707 
detected genes were removed using filter_cells, and genes expressed in fewer than 3 cells were 708 
removed using filter_genes. Cells with total UMI counts greater than 25,000 were also removed 709 
to limit the inclusion of doublets. CellBender -filtered raw UMI counts were normalized to 10,000 710 
UMI per cell using normalize_total, then log-transformed with log1p. The top 2,000 highly variable 711 
genes were selected with highly_variable_genes. For two -dimensional visualization, we 712 
embedded the cells with UMAP using the top 50 principal components; all other parameters were 713 
left at their defaults. Cell type annotations were transferred from the original work 2. The cluster 714 
annotated as myeloid cells was reassigned as macrophages, and FDCs were split and annotated 715 
as either FDCs or MRCs based on known marker genes. 716 
Stereo-seq mouse brain data 717 
The Stereo-seq mouse samples were processed with Scanpy57. The original binning of the beads 718 
was kept. Whole embryo slices were cropped to keep only the brain. Cells with fewer than 100 719 
detected genes were removed using filter_cells, and genes expressed in fewer than 3 cells were 720 
removed using filter_genes. Raw UMI counts were normalized to 10,000 UMI per cell using 721 
normalize_total, then log -transformed with log1p. The leiden function was used to cluster the 722 
binned cells, and the resulting clusters were annotated as in the original works according to their 723 
anatomical regions. If the original annotation was available it was kept, leiden resolution was 724 
chosen to achieve clear separation. Upper and deep layers were separated according to the 725 
clustering based on known layer specific markers. 726 
Analysis with LARIS 727 
Slide-tags human tonsil data 728 
To calculate the integrated LR scores for each cell, we applied the prepareLRInteraction function 729 
from LARIS (number_nearest_neighbors=20). Interactions with spatial specificity and variability, 730 
relative to randomly shuffled locations, were identified using the runLARIS function 731 
(n_nearest_neighbors=20, mu=0.25, n_repeats=5, sigma=100). To infer and rank interactions at 732 
the cluster level, we employed the _calculate_laris_score_by_celltype function (mu=100, 733 
mask_threshold=1e-6) within the runLARIS function. To cluster B germinal centre cells by their 734 
interactions, we first filtered the cluster -level predictions to the top 3,000 highest -ranked 735 
interactions and selected those LR pairs in which B germinal centre cells were either senders or 736 
receivers, yielding a total of 161 interactions. The B germinal centre cells were then subset, their 737 
LR scores log-transformed, and PCA and UMAP were constructed on the LR scores with default 738 
parameters. The leiden function was used to cluster the cells (resolution=1.1), and the resulting 739 
clusters were assigned to dark or light zones based on known marker genes. To visualize the DZ 740 
(‘CXCR4’, ‘AICDA’, ‘FOXP1’, ‘MME’) and LZ (‘CD83’, ‘LMO2’, ‘BCL2A1’) genes as modules, we 741 
used the score_genes function. Regionally enriched interactions were identified with COSG 742 
(mu=100, expressed_pct=0.15, remove_lowly_expressed=True, n_genes_user=100) 61. To 743

different developmental time points and spatial locations, we applied COSG (mu=100, 761 
expressed_pct=0.05, remove_lowly_expressed=True, n_genes_user=250) to the regional 762 
annotations. To quantify changes in interaction strength in the dorsal-ventral direction, the tissue 763 
slices were first oriented to be parallel with the x-axis, then the LR scores were projected into 2D. 764

midline, then the LR scores were projected into 2D along the y-axis. Gene set enrichment analysis 766

receptors before the test. 771

"""End-to-end integration test based on the LARIS tutorial.

Uses the tonsil dataset (5,695 cells x 25,583 genes, 14 cell types) and
the bundled CellChatDB human database to run the full LARIS pipeline:

    load data → prepareLRInteraction → runLARIS → plotting functions

This mirrors the official tutorial at:
    https://genecell.github.io/LARIS/notebooks/04_LARIS_tutorial.html

Data location (checked in order):
    1. $LARIS_TEST_DATA environment variable (path to directory containing
       adata_tonsil.h5ad)
    2. Default: tests/data/ relative to the repo root

Set the environment variable to point at your local copy, e.g.:
    export LARIS_TEST_DATA=/data1/mdai/Result/single-cell/Methods/LARIS/tutorial

If the file is absent the entire module is skipped.
"""

import os
import warnings

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # non-interactive backend for CI

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest
import scanpy as sc
import scipy.sparse as sp

import laris as la

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Skip the entire module if the tutorial dataset is not available
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
_REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(__file__))
_DEFAULT_DATA_DIR = os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, "tests", "data")
_DATA_DIR = os.environ.get("LARIS_TEST_DATA", _DEFAULT_DATA_DIR)
_ADATA_PATH = os.path.join(_DATA_DIR, "adata_tonsil.h5ad")

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(
    not os.path.isfile(_ADATA_PATH),
    reason="Tutorial dataset not found (adata_tonsil.h5ad)",
)


# =========================================================================
# Fixtures — heavy computation, cached for the whole module
# =========================================================================

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def adata():
    """Load the tonsil AnnData."""
    return sc.read_h5ad(_ADATA_PATH)


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
